summary:
Nāgāland stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, and no deviation from the national position has been identified for the state at a margin material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Nāgāland therefore faces the same recognition, documentation and policing conditions as elsewhere in India.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, narrows the 2019 definition of transgender person, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. Human Rights Watch called the bill a major reversal of the 2014 rights and urged the president not to sign it (26 March 2026). Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist.

The bill has been approved by both houses of Parliament and was awaiting presidential assent at the time of writing. The government argues that the narrower definition improves delivery of welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Critics warn that it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people, and they describe mandatory medical certification as an attack on privacy and dignity. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The amendment reverses a recognition baseline that had been in place since 2014: the Supreme Court's third-gender ruling established self-identification, and the 2019 Act that Parliament amended had been built on it. The direction of travel is therefore towards narrower recognition, while judicial intervention has moved in the opposite direction on questions of policing and medical practice.

Two accounts of the same measure compete. The government presents the narrower definition as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; Human Rights Watch, activists and critics quoted in the press present it as a denial of recognition to the majority of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. The sources do not resolve this dispute.

Legislative status is unsettled as written: the bill has cleared both houses but has not been signed, and Human Rights Watch has addressed its appeal directly to the president. Whether assent follows, and on what terms it is implemented, is not sourced here.

The 2024 change to the penal code is a distinct deterioration from the amendment, affecting sexual-violence protection rather than recognition, and it applies nationwide including in Nāgāland.

Nāgāland's own position is not distinguished from the national score; the state's assessment rests on national sources, and any state-level deviation would have to be evidenced separately.
localsOnly:
Residents of Nāgāland seeking legal recognition of gender identity must meet the amended national test: recognition is confined to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, supported by medical certification. Self-identification alone no longer suffices.

Trans, non-binary and gender-fluid residents who identify outside the accepted categories have no route to recognition under the amended scheme, which affects identity documents and, on the government's own framing, access to welfare schemes.

Residents reporting sexual violence face a code that no longer carries the gender-identity-specific offences present in the Indian Penal Code; trans communities have reported fear of a rise in assaults under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

Protection machinery runs through the courts. The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police direct police sensitisation, bar conversion therapy, and bind the National Medical Commission and education authorities, and the Allahabad High Court ordered relief in February 2026 against a mandatory medical examination for a passport applicant.

Same-sex relationships are lawful following the 2018 Supreme Court judgment, but marriage and civil partnership are unavailable to same-sex couples, and discrimination on grounds including sex is barred under an interpretation that covers gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether presidential assent has since been given to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill is unresolved in these sources; the inventory records the bill as approved by both houses and awaiting assent.

No Nāgāland-specific incident involving a trans traveller, document applicant or person in police custody is sourced here; the checkpoint findings come from other Indian states and are used to indicate a national pattern.

Whether Nāgāland's police or transport authorities have issued their own instructions on gender verification is not sourced, and the state's own record on implementation remains unverified.

The scope of the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines outside that state is not stated in the inventory; they are cited as the strongest documented judicial intervention rather than as a binding rule for Nāgāland.

The claim that the 2026 amendment applies retroactively to documents already issued, or to residents recognised before March 2026, is not addressed by any source here and should be treated as unresolved.
